title: Stateless auth with JWT
idea: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a signed string of claims, such as a user's id and role. The server signs it at login, then only verifies it.

analogy.text: A festival wristband with a tamper-proof seal. Staff check the seal and read the colour; they keep no guest list.
analogy.breaks: You cannot cancel one early without keeping a list, which brings state back.

points: At login the server signs the claims with a secret and returns the token.
The client sends it with every request as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
`jwt.verify` recomputes the signature and checks `exp`, the expiry time.
Stateless means no stored login: any server holding the secret can verify it.

steps.caption: The login response carries a token: header, payload and signature, joined by dots.
Header and payload are only encoded. Anyone can read `sub` (the user id), `role` and `exp`.
The signature is a fingerprint of the first two parts, made with the secret. The secret stays on the server.
A client edits `role` to `admin`. The old signature no longer matches, so `jwt.verify` throws.
Only a holder of the secret can sign an edited payload that the server accepts.

code.title: Sign and verify
code.caption: `verify` returns the claims only for an untouched, unexpired token signed with the same secret.

code.title: Login and a stateless route
code.caption: Login queries Postgres once. After that, `authenticate` needs no database at all.

walk.text: Setup: a demo `JWT_SECRET` and a `users` table holding Ada. The low bcrypt cost keeps the demo fast.
Look up the user and compare the password with the stored hash. Both failures give one message.
Sign the claims with the secret from the environment. The token expires in 15 minutes.
`authenticate` strips `Bearer ` and verifies the token, accepting only HS256.
A bad or missing token ends the request with `401`. A good one fills `req.user`.
The route reads the claims from `req.user`. It runs no query.
Close the database pool first. The token still works; a request without one gets `401`.

pitfalls: Never put passwords or private data in the payload; anyone can decode it.
Always set `expiresIn`; a token without an expiry works forever.
Keep `JWT_SECRET` in the environment. Anyone who has it can mint admin tokens.

quiz.why: `jwt.decode` only reads the payload, so the forged `admin` shows. `jwt.verify` recomputes the signature, finds a mismatch and throws.

takeaway: The token carries its own proof, so the server stores nothing per login.

starters: How is a JWT different from a session cookie?
